learningObjectives.title: Tectonic hazards (earthquakes, volcanoes and plate margins)
Weather hazards (tropical storms and UK extreme weather)

questions.q: Which statement best defines a natural hazard?
options: A natural event that threatens people or has the potential to cause damage, destruction and death
A man-made event that harms only the natural environment
Any change in the weather that lasts less than a day
The amount of money a country spends after a disaster
questions.explain: A natural hazard is a naturally occurring event that poses a threat to people or property.

questions.q: What is meant by 'hazard risk'?
options: The probability or chance that a natural hazard may take place
The total number of people killed by a disaster
The cost of rebuilding after an event
A natural event that has no impact on people
questions.explain: Hazard risk is the probability of a population being affected by a natural hazard.

questions.q: Which factor is most likely to increase a population's hazard risk?
options: Rapid urbanisation concentrating people in hazard-prone areas
A declining and widely dispersed rural population
Strict building regulations that are well enforced
High wealth and very low levels of poverty
questions.explain: Urbanisation concentrates people and property, increasing the number exposed to a hazard.

questions.q: At which type of plate margin do two plates move apart?
questions.explain: At a constructive (divergent) margin plates move apart and rising magma forms new crust.

questions.q: The San Andreas Fault in California is an example of which plate margin?
questions.explain: At the San Andreas Fault two plates slide past one another at a conservative margin.

questions.q: At a destructive plate margin, why does the oceanic plate sink beneath the continental plate?
options: Oceanic crust is denser than continental crust
Continental crust is denser than oceanic crust
Oceanic crust is much thicker than continental crust
The two plates are actually moving apart
questions.explain: The denser oceanic crust is subducted beneath the less dense continental crust.

questions.q: A village sits on fertile soils on the slopes of an active volcano. Which reason best explains why people choose to live there?
options: Weathered volcanic material creates fertile soils that are good for farming
Living beside a volcano removes all risk of natural hazards
Volcanoes prevent earthquakes from ever happening nearby
Volcanic areas are guaranteed never to erupt again
questions.explain: Volcanic areas attract settlement through fertile soils, geothermal energy, minerals and tourism.

questions.q: Which of the following is a secondary effect of an earthquake?
options: Fires started by ruptured gas mains
Buildings collapsing as the ground shakes
People injured by falling debris during the quake
questions.explain: Secondary effects occur later as a consequence of the primary effects, such as fires from broken gas pipes.

questions.q: Which of these is an immediate (short-term) response to an earthquake?
options: Search and rescue of trapped survivors
Introducing stricter building regulations for the future
Attracting long-term investment to rebuild the economy
questions.explain: Immediate responses happen in the hours and days after an event, such as rescuing and treating survivors.

questions.q: Scientists install seismometers around a volcano to record ground movement before an eruption. Which risk-reduction strategy is this?
questions.explain: Monitoring uses instruments such as seismometers to record the warning signs of a tectonic hazard.

questions.q: What is the minimum sea surface temperature usually required for a tropical storm to form?
questions.explain: Tropical storms typically form over oceans warmer than about 27°C.

questions.q: Between which latitudes do tropical storms generally form?
options: Between 5° and 30° north and south of the Equator
Only poleward of the Arctic and Antarctic Circles
questions.explain: Tropical storms form roughly 5° to 30° north and south, where seas are warm and the Coriolis effect is sufficient.

questions.q: What is the name of the calm, clear area at the centre of a tropical storm?
questions.explain: The eye is the calm centre where air descends, surrounded by the eyewall of strongest winds.

questions.q: Why is there generally a belt of low pressure at the Equator?
options: Intense solar heating causes warm air to rise
Cold air is constantly sinking towards the surface
Winds are permanently absent from the region
The oceans there are too cold for any evaporation
questions.explain: Strong heating at the Equator makes warm air rise, creating a low-pressure belt.

questions.q: Which scale is used to measure the strength of a tropical storm?
questions.explain: The Saffir-Simpson scale grades tropical storms from category 1 to 5 based on wind speed.

questions.q: Climate scientists forecast warmer ocean temperatures in the future. What is the most likely effect on tropical storms?
options: Their intensity is likely to increase
They will only form over the poles
Their wind speeds will fall to zero
questions.explain: Warmer oceans supply more energy, so climate change is expected to increase the intensity of tropical storms.

questions.q: The current geological period, covering roughly the last 2.6 million years, is called the...
questions.explain: The Quaternary period spans the last 2.6 million years and is studied to understand climate change.

questions.q: Which natural cause of climate change involves long-term changes in the Earth's orbit and axial tilt?
questions.explain: Milankovitch cycles describe changes in the Earth's orbit (eccentricity), axial tilt and precession.

questions.q: Which greenhouse gas is released in the greatest quantity when fossil fuels are burned?
questions.explain: Burning fossil fuels releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, the main greenhouse gas from human activity.

questions.q: A coastal town builds higher sea walls to cope with rising sea levels. This is an example of which climate change management approach?
questions.explain: Adaptation means responding to the effects of climate change, such as defending coasts against rising seas.
